_about: The public demo's sample deck: original cards on a mix of subjects, written for this project (no third-party course material). Cards with a 'template' get fresh numbers every time: their question and answer are generated from it, with the 'original' values used for the first version and for the start-up checks.

cards.question: What is the forgetting curve?
cards.answer: It's the pattern, first measured by Hermann Ebbinghaus in the 1880s, that we forget new information quickly at first and then more slowly. Without review, much of what you learn is gone within days. Each well-timed review makes the curve flatter, so the memory lasts longer before it fades again.

cards.question: Why does spaced repetition beat cramming?
cards.answer: Reviewing just as you're starting to forget strengthens a memory far more than reviewing something you still remember easily. Spacing reviews out, with gaps that grow each time you succeed, gives you those effortful recalls. Cramming packs reviews together, so it works for tomorrow's test but fades quickly afterwards.

cards.question: What is the testing effect, and how is it different from rereading?
cards.answer: The testing effect is the finding that actively pulling information out of memory, by answering questions or recalling without looking, strengthens it much more than rereading. Rereading feels productive because the material looks familiar, but recognising something is not the same as being able to produce it.

cards.question: Why does explaining something in your own words help you learn it?
cards.answer: Putting an idea into your own words forces you to connect it to what you already know, which makes it easier to recall later. It also exposes gaps: if you can't explain it simply, you haven't fully understood it yet. This is the idea behind the Feynman technique.

cards.question: In the Zhuangzi, what does Wheelwright Bian tell Duke Huan about the books he is reading?
cards.answer: That they are only the dregs of the men of old. Bian can feel the knack of making a wheel in his hands, but he can't put it into words, so he couldn't even pass it on to his own son, and is still making wheels at seventy. Real skill comes from practice, not from reading about it.

cards.question: Why is the sky blue?
cards.answer: Sunlight contains all colours. As it passes through the atmosphere, air molecules scatter short wavelengths, like blue, much more strongly than long ones, like red (Rayleigh scattering). That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky. Violet is scattered even more, but the sun emits less of it and our eyes are less sensitive to it.

cards.question: What causes the seasons?
cards.answer: The tilt of Earth's axis, about 23.4 degrees. As Earth orbits the sun, each hemisphere spends part of the year tilted towards it, getting more direct sunlight and longer days (summer), and part tilted away (winter). It isn't distance from the sun: Earth is actually closest to the sun in early January.

cards.question: What's the difference between a bacterium and a virus?
cards.answer: A bacterium is a living single-celled organism that can feed and reproduce on its own; antibiotics can kill many bacteria. A virus is much smaller and isn't a cell at all: it can only copy itself by getting inside a host's cells. That's why antibiotics don't work on viruses.

cards.question: In a sentence or two, what does DNA do?
cards.answer: DNA stores the instructions for building and running an organism. Its sequence of bases is read in groups of three, through RNA, to make proteins, and it is copied and passed on to offspring.

cards.question: What is the placebo effect, and why do drug trials use a control group?
cards.answer: The placebo effect is a real improvement people feel after a treatment with no active ingredient, because they expect to get better. Trials compare the drug with a placebo given to a control group, ideally with neither patients nor doctors knowing who got which, so that any extra benefit can be credited to the drug itself.

cards.question: What is the Rosetta Stone, and why did it matter?
cards.answer: It's an Egyptian stone slab from 196 BC carrying the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and ancient Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek, it gave them the key to deciphering hieroglyphs, which Jean-François Champollion achieved in 1822.

cards.question: Why was Gutenberg's printing press such a big deal?
cards.answer: Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type with a press, so books could be produced quickly and cheaply instead of copied by hand. Ideas spread faster and further than ever, literacy grew, and the press helped fuel the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

cards.question: What was the Silk Road?
cards.answer: Not one road but a network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe, active from around the 2nd century BC. Silk, spices and other goods travelled along it, and so did ideas, religions, technologies and diseases.

cards.question: What is the Socratic method?
cards.answer: A way of teaching and thinking by asking questions instead of giving answers. By questioning someone's beliefs step by step, you expose hidden assumptions and contradictions, so they reach a clearer understanding themselves.

template.question: A price rises from ${old} to ${new}. What is the percentage increase?
template.answer:
Change = ${new} − ${old} = ${diff}
Percentage increase = change ÷ original price = ${diff} ÷ ${old} = {pct:.1f}%

template.question: A jacket costs ${p}. It's {d}% off, and then {t}% sales tax is added. What do you pay?
You drive {d} km at {v1} km/h, then another {d} km at {v2} km/h. What is your average speed for the whole trip?
template.answer:
Time = {d} ÷ {v1} + {d} ÷ {v2} = {t1:.2f} + {t2:.2f} = {tt:.2f} hours
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = {dist} km ÷ {tt:.2f} h = {avg:.1f} km/h

It isn't the simple average of the two speeds, because you spend longer driving at the slower one.

template.question: Using the rule of 72, roughly how many years does an investment take to double at {r}% a year? How close is that to the exact answer?
template.answer:
Rule of 72: 72 ÷ {r} ≈ {approx:.1f} years
Exact: ln 2 ÷ ln(1 + {r}%) = {exact:.1f} years, so the shortcut is very close at everyday interest rates.

cards.question: In plain words, what is compound interest?
cards.answer: Interest that is earned on your earlier interest as well as on the original amount. Each year's growth is added to the balance, so the next year's interest is calculated on a bigger number. Over long periods this snowballing makes a huge difference, which is why starting early matters.

cards.question: What is inflation, and what does it do to money sitting in a savings account?
cards.answer: Inflation is the general rise in prices over time, so each dollar buys a little less each year. If your savings earn less interest than the inflation rate, their real value, what they can actually buy, shrinks even though the balance goes up.

cards.question: Why does diversification reduce risk?
cards.answer: Different investments don't all go up and down at the same time. Holding many of them means the losses on some are often offset by gains on others, so the overall result swings less than any single investment would. It reduces the risk specific to individual investments, but not the risk of the whole market falling together.
